book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

chapters.relation: The chapter asks whether Fallout's chems should be banned and answers no on Millian grounds: chem addiction harms only the user (and is trivially curable at any wasteland doctor, unlike Cait's Psycho addiction in Fallout 4, which shows what real addiction actually costs), so the New California Republic's firing squads for chem dealers and Caesar's Legion's crucifixion of the smuggler Anders violate the Harm Principle. Combat chem use is self-protection, drugging a Charisma check harms no one because NPCs act on their own programmed preferences, and paternalism fares no better in a wasteland where a failed speech check can get you killed. The analysis then extends to real-world performance-enhancing drugs: permissible for soldiers fighting a just war, but coercive in sports, where PED users force clean athletes to choose between their own health risks.

When Lucy shouts the Golden Rule at the Ghoul after he dunks her in a poison river to bait a gulper, the chapter takes her appeal seriously and grades the rival 'rules' of the wasteland (the Iron, Arsenic, Neon, and Bronze Rules) before arguing the Golden Rule needs St. Francis's 'in a similar situation' clause. Kant's criminal-versus-judge objection disqualifies the unqualified Platinum Rule of treating others as they want, Nietzsche's charge that mutual restraint denies life is parried, and Rawlsian imagining of ourselves in divergent positions explains why family partiality like Lucy's search for Hank is consistent with the rule. The chapter closes with Lucy's saving of the Ghoul retold as the Good Samaritan parable, extending the rule even to enemies.

The chapter maps four schools of ethics onto Fallout 4's Commonwealth: Aristotle's virtue ethics reads Preston Garvey's settlement defense as the mean between recklessness and cowardice and temperance as moderate chem use; Kant's Categorical Imperative is tested on stealing ammo in Concord and on the Battle of Bunker Hill choice to warn the Railroad, where loyal silence to Father fails universalization and treats synths merely as means. Aquinas's natural law ethics, keyed to the telos of power armor, workbenches, and Pip-Boys, condemns the Institute's creation of synths by analogy to the IVF debate while still demanding dignity for synths who already exist. Finally, Bentham's utilitarianism is the one framework under which Father's Institute — adaptive labor force, scientific progress, stability and order — can sincerely believe itself morally justified.

Tracing Fallout's own censorship history — the GURPS licensing cancellation threat, the invisibility of child NPCs in the European release, the moral panic after Columbine — the chapter asks whether it is wrong to simulate evil, framing the issue with Morgan Luck's gamer's dilemma. Plato's cave and the Forms ground the 'media impacts morals' worry: games are shadows of shadows whose simulated vice accumulates 'a large evil in our souls', which is also why Lucy's Vault upbringing leaves her underprepared for the wasteland's emotions. Against this, Aristotle's catharsis and Schulzke's claim that Fallout trains phronesis support depicting wrongdoing as practice for moral judgment, so the chapter concludes the right wrongs to depict are whichever maximize the simulation of choice, with Braun's player-controlled Tranquility Lane simulation as the dystopian counter-model.

Weighing Vault-Tec's secret experiments — Vault 11's yearly human sacrifice, Vault 13's 200-year lockdown, the cryogenic freezing of the Sole Survivor — the chapter asks whether the ends could ever justify the vaults. On Kant's Universal Law and Humanity Formulations the answer is flatly no: dwellers were deceived into becoming mere means to data, whatever the hypothetical space-colonization motive that designer Tim Cain favors. Act and rule utilitarianism in Bentham's tradition give a more equivocal verdict — exposed deception would doom any future cooperation, yet safeguarding humanity might in extraordinary circumstances tip the calculus — and the chapter situates the games in real research-ethics history from the eugenics era to the Tuskegee study and the Belmont Report.

chapters.file: ch30 - Part 5 A BEAUTIFUL DISASTER THE AESTHETICS OF FALLOUT.md

chapters.relation: The chapter asks why Fallout's genre fusion — RPG plus first-person shooter plus post-apocalyptic Western plus black comedy — coheres rather than collapses, and answers with Kendall Walton's 'Categories of Art': works carry standard, variable, and contra-standard properties relative to each category they belong to, so every added category raises the number of expectations a designer must meet. C. Thi Nguyen's account of games as prescribing striving play explains why obstacle-free software would not even count as a game, while a hypothetical forced Moby-Dick book-report quest illustrates a contra-standard property that 'does violence' to the category. Fallout's S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system implicitly promises 'play how you want', so weak melee builds or underused speech skills are aesthetic risk — the designer's gamble that players will recognize every fused genre at once.

The chapter argues modding is the deepest freedom Bethesda-era Fallout offers: Sartre and Beauvoir's absolute freedom and facticity explain why vanilla players merely pick among given priorities while modders inject new meaning into the game, constrained but not determined by the Creation Engine. Spinoza's causal determinism becomes a model of 'immanent freedom' — just as Spinoza's agent is free by understanding their place in Nature's web of causes, the modder is free by grasping how they fit into the load orders, plugin files, and tools of the Creation Kit. Simone Weil's ideal of self-directed labor culminates the argument: Fallout: London's five-year, unpaid total conversion (the Atta-Boy, Churchill the bulldog, the punk-anarchist Pistols) embodies the convergence of thought and action that Moira Brown's line about putting broken glass back together captures.

The chapter argues Fallout 4's grip comes not from graphical fidelity but from first-person moral agency: deciding the fate of Gen 3 synths who do not know they are synths — supporting their escape, hunting them, or installing them as unwitting spies — forces the player through emotionally real moral deliberation. It connects this to Turing's worry about proving to another that you think ('it could've been me in their shoes') and to Nagel's bat, proposing that imagining what it is like to be a synth is a stepping stone toward ever stranger perspectives. Playing thus becomes the joy of actually doing philosophy — reawakening imagination, reshuffling our space of possibilities, and returning us to our own problems refreshed rather than merely escaped.

Against the complaint that Fallout 3 is just Morrowind or Oblivion with a post-apocalyptic coat of paint, the chapter tests three aesthetic theories. Aristotle's didactic mimesis explains the tragic 'war never changes' framing and its moral lessons about resource wars and the AI president John Henry Eden, while Francis Hutcheson's 'uniformity amidst variety' locates Fallout's fun in the orderly S.P.E.C.I.A.L. rules and the 'crunch' of complex gear and crafting. Clive Bell's formalism finally secures the difference: Vault Boy's atomic-age cartoon style, the Pip-Boy's green monochrome, and the western motifs are formal properties no Elder Scrolls game shares, making Fallout 3 a formally distinct artwork to be appreciated for its own sake.

The chapter rereads Fallout 3's original Project Purity ending — the forced walk into the lethal radiation chamber while radiation-immune followers Fawkes, Sergeant RL-3, and Charon each refuse — as the game's worst case of narrative paradox: the pre-authored story compels an action the player-authored character narrative cannot accommodate. On the narrative-identity view (mounted against Galen Strawson's denial of narrativity), the Karma system and companions like Fawkes matter through the story the player tells, so an evil, greed-driven Lone Wanderer dying nobly is a 'bad death' that unravels the motivation for the entire playthrough. Dying well requires death to fit the story, and Sarah Lyons's substitutable sacrifice — or a last-page redemption epiphany — is what restores narrative coherence.

Opening from the author's own grief — she nearly stopped playing Fallout 4 because its murdered spouse and kidnapped son echoed the loss of her real infant son — the chapter applies the ethics of care of Gilligan, Noddings, and Tronto to Fallout's wasteland. Care relationships structure the games: the Fallout 3 father whose flight from Vault 101 propels the plot, Dogmeat's loyal responsiveness as relational reciprocity, and the Fallout 4 son Shaun, where caring for your child collides with caring for a Commonwealth his Institute endangers. Settlement-building, faction choice (Lyons's Brotherhood handing out clean water versus the Railroad's liberation of synths), and even the Black Widow perk path that saves Megaton all become care-laden moral acts — care as protest against the wasteland's ethos of bare survival.

The chapter asks why audiences relish stories of civilization's end and answers with psychology: the wasteland is Hobbes's 'nasty, brutish, and short' (raiders abducting Hank, Vault-Tec's experiments on dwellers), yet Ernest Becker's death-denial and Maslow's hierarchy of needs explain the appeal — fiction lets us confront mortality safely while watching characters meet needs for security, control, and meaning. The show's scenes carry the argument: the Vault 33 Council suppressing Lucy's search party trades freedom for safety, Maximus letting Titus bleed out reclaims control of his destiny, and Lucy's gift of life-sustaining vials to the unconscious Ghoul models hope and retained humanity. Apocalypse originally means 'an uncovering', so these narratives reveal what viewers value and let them rehearse their own endings.

Why is living in Fallout's hell — ghouls pouring through the ceiling, radroach dinners, Kellogg, Pickman, Vault-Tec — fun? The chapter tests the two classic solutions to the puzzle of dark art: Aristotle's katharsis works for Oedipus but stumbles because playing is actively enjoyable rather than unpleasant purgation, and RPGs blur feeling pity for a character with fear for oneself; Hume's 'Of Tragedy' account, on which artistic skill transforms negative emotions into pleasure by mixing them with beauty, fails because the wasteland is deliberately ugly, not beautiful, and Hume never explains how the transformation works. Neither the ancient nor the modern answer quite succeeds, so the 2,500-year-old puzzle is left open, like the best unfinished quests.

holes.name: The Gamer's Dilemma
holes.what: Morgan Luck's puzzle that anyone who thinks simulating virtual murder is permissible lacks a principled reason to condemn simulating other virtual wrongs such as virtual child abuse.
holes.why: Chapter 28 builds its whole defense of Fallout's depiction of evil around this dilemma, concluding developers should depict whichever wrongs maximize simulated choice.

holes.name: Kendall Walton
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of art whose 'Categories of Art' holds that a work's aesthetic properties depend on the standard, variable, and contra-standard properties of the categories it belongs to.
holes.why: Chapter 31's entire account of Fallout's genre fusion and aesthetic risk is an application of Walton's category theory.

holes.name: Categories of Art (standard, variable and contra-standard properties)
holes.what: Walton's framework on which artworks are judged relative to art categories whose standard properties qualify membership and whose contra-standard properties disqualify it.
holes.why: Chapter 31 uses it to explain how Fallout can be simultaneously RPG, shooter, post-apocalyptic comedy, and why each added genre is an aesthetic gamble.

holes.name: Simone Weil
holes.what: French philosopher and mystic who defined freedom as the convergence of thought and action, achieved above all through self-directed labor.
holes.why: Chapter 32 uses Weil's account of free creative labor to explain why the unpaid five-year Fallout: London mod is the fullest expression of freedom.

holes.name: Francis Hutcheson
holes.what: Scottish Enlightenment philosopher who grounded beauty in an internal sense responding to 'uniformity amidst variety'.
holes.why: Chapter 34 uses Hutcheson's theory to explain the aesthetic pleasure of Fallout's orderly S.P.E.C.I.A.L. rules and gameplay 'crunch'.

holes.name: Clive Bell
holes.what: Art critic and formalist who held that art's value lies in 'significant form' — arrangements of line and color that evoke a distinctive aesthetic emotion.
holes.why: Chapter 34 uses Bell's formalism to show Fallout 3's atomic-age style (Vault Boy, Pip-Boy green, western motifs) makes it a formally distinct artwork, not a reskinned Elder Scrolls game.

holes.name: Catharsis (purgation of pity and fear)
holes.what: Aristotle's Poetics account of tragedy arousing pity and fear in order to purge or perfect those emotions in the audience.
holes.why: Chapter 34 appeals to catharsis to explain how Fallout 3's dark themes deliver moral and emotional benefits.

holes.name: Narrative Identity and Narrative Ethics
holes.what: The view that who we are and what we ought to do is grounded in the life-story we author from our interpreted past events.
holes.why: Chapter 35 argues Fallout 3's forced sacrificial ending is a bad death because it disrupts the player-authored character narrative that motivates play.

holes.name: Galen Strawson
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher who argues 'against narrativity', denying that a good life requires understanding oneself as a continuous story.
holes.why: Chapter 35 uses Strawson's skepticism about narrative identity as the main objection to its story-based account of RPG motivation.

holes.name: Ernest Becker
holes.what: Cultural anthropologist whose The Denial of Death holds that terror of mortality drives human striving and symbolic-immortality projects.
holes.why: Chapter 38 frames the appeal of post-apocalyptic fiction as a safe confrontation with the death-anxiety Becker described.

holes.name: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
holes.what: Humanist psychology's model on which physiological and safety needs must be met before belonging, esteem, and self-actualization become salient.
holes.why: Chapter 38 explains Fallout's appeal through characters' struggles to meet each level of the hierarchy in the wasteland.

holes.name: The Paradox of Tragedy (the attraction of dark art)
holes.what: The puzzle of why we enjoy depictions of suffering and horror in art that we would hate to experience in real life.
holes.why: Chapter 39 is organized around this puzzle — why players enjoy Fallout's hellish wasteland — and tests Aristotle's and Hume's solutions against it.

holes.name: Catharsis (purgation of pity and fear)
holes.what: Aristotle's Poetics account of tragedy arousing pity and fear to purge or perfect them in the audience.
holes.why: Chapter 39 tests katharsis as an explanation of why playing a horrific wasteland is fun and finds it wanting.
